outcome: No event since 26 January 2024 settles or moves the question. No composite c with 2^c − 1 ≡ 1 (mod c²) is known, and none is ruled out; the problem remains open, and for odd c it is equivalent to the open question whether a base-2 Wieferich pseudoprime exists.
problem_asks: Whether there exists a composite integer c with 2^c − 1 ≡ 1 (mod c²). Parts: (1) the domain is composite integers c; (2) the congruence, equivalently 2^c ≡ 2 (mod c²), i.e. c² divides 2^c − 2; (3) the question is existence only, yes or no. It asks for no bound, count, construction or classification. Restatements worked out from the statement alone: even c never satisfy it for c ≥ 4 (4 divides c² while 2^c − 2 ≡ 2 mod 4), so only odd c matter; for odd c the congruence is 2^(c−1) ≡ 1 (mod c²), which is a base-2 'Wieferich pseudoprime' in the terminology of OEIS A298944.

events.what_happened: F. G. Dorais and D. Klyve, 'A Wieferich Prime Search up to 6.7 × 10^15', Journal of Integer Sequences 14 (2011), art. 11.9.2. Reports that no Wieferich primes p < 6.7 × 10^15 exist besides 1093 and 3511 (p² divides 2^(p−1) − 1). It is about primes, not composite c. No earlier preprint was found, so the date given is the journal publication. A search snippet gave 16 Oct 2011 as the publication day and 30 Jun 2011 as the receipt date; I did not verify those on the journal page, so the precision is month.
events.delivers: Among primes below 6.7 × 10^15, only 1093 and 3511 satisfy p² | 2^(p−1) − 1. Every prime factor of a composite solution c must satisfy this (see summary), so any solution whose prime factors are all below 6.7 × 10^15 can only be built from 1093 and 3511. This restricts candidates; it does not decide whether any composite c exists.
events.remains: All of problem_asks. The existence question for composite c is untouched, including any c with a prime factor above 6.7 × 10^15.

checked_by.who: F. G. Dorais (University of Michigan) and D. Klyve (Central Washington University)
checked_by.qualification: The authors of the computation, publishing in a refereed journal.
checked_by.what_they_did: Ran the search and published the method (double-precision Montgomery arithmetic with a memoryless sieve). I did not read a referee statement; refereeing is implied by journal publication only.

events.directly_checkable: The two primes can be checked by hand as p² | 2^(p−1) − 1 for p = 1093 and p = 3511; the values are quoted in OEIS A001567 and Wikipedia, and I did not recompute them. The absence below 6.7 × 10^15 is a computer search whose method is described in the paper; I did not re-run it.
events.direction: Restricts rather than decides. It limits which primes can divide a composite solution. It does not cut for or against existence.

events.what_happened: PrimeGrid's volunteer Wieferich search is reported as completed to 2^64 (about 1.8 × 10^19) as of 29 Dec 2022, with no plans to continue. The statement comes from a comment by Charles R Greathouse IV on OEIS A001220, dated 24 Sep 2024. Wikipedia's Wieferich prime article says a third Wieferich prime must exceed 2^64, citing PrimeGrid's 'WW Statistics'. The PrimeGrid page itself was not opened. Earlier OEIS comments by Max Alekseyev (20 Nov 2015) report a milestone of 4.97 × 10^17, say the results were not double-checked, and note that the search was suspended in May 2017 because of unreliable testing and resumed on 28 Nov 2020.
events.revisions: Completion date restated in OEIS A001220 comment of 24 Sep 2024. Earlier milestones: 2015 (4.97 × 10^17), search suspended May 2017, resumed Nov 2020.
events.delivers: Reported: no Wieferich prime below 2^64 other than 1093 and 3511. Consequence for the question: any composite solution below 2^64 has every prime factor in {1093, 3511}. A composite solution at or above 2^64 would need a prime factor above 2^64 that is a Wieferich prime, and none is known. This restricts candidates; it does not decide existence.
events.remains: All of problem_asks, including every composite c whose prime factors include a Wieferich prime above 2^64.
events.time_since_posted: about 3 years 9 months to the most recent written restatement I found (OEIS, Sep 2024); no independent verification found
events.directly_checkable: The 2^64 absence is a long distributed computation. I found no independent re-run of it. The 6.7 × 10^15 search of Dorais and Klyve is independently published and is the only checkable part.
events.doubts: Alekseyev's OEIS comment of 20 Nov 2015 says the PrimeGrid results 'were not double-checked' and that 'because of the unreliability of the testing, the search was suspended in May 2017'. It resumed on 28 Nov 2020. The 2^64 completion therefore rests on a volunteer run whose testing reliability was questioned by an OEIS editor, and I found no independent check of it. Both the 2015 comment and the 2024 restatement are in OEIS, which is not itself a verification.
events.direction: Indirect. If the run is correct, it narrows the prime factors any composite solution could have. It does not cut for or against existence.
people: PrimeGrid volunteer project (no individual named for the 2^64 completion in what I read)

events.what_happened: Non-squarefree base-2 pseudoprimes were checked up to 10^12 (R. G. E. Pinch, 'The pseudoprimes up to 10^13', ANTS-IV, 2000) and up to 25 × 10^9 (P. Ribenboim, The Little Book of Bigger Primes, 2004, p. 99). As Wikipedia's Wieferich prime article reports them, the only repeated prime factors found are 1093 and 3511. Neither primary source was opened. This is recorded from Wikipedia's citations, which I did read.
events.delivers: For base-2 pseudoprimes up to 10^12, the only repeated prime factors p with p² dividing the pseudoprime are 1093 and 3511 (Ribenboim: up to 25 × 10^9). Applied here, a non-squarefree composite solution below 10^12 would have to be built from 1093 and 3511. It does not cover squarefree candidates, which need the Wieferich-prime argument in the summary, so this is not a complete finite check of the congruence.
events.remains: All of problem_asks beyond that restricted class: squarefree candidates, and every c at or above 10^12 (or 25 × 10^9 for Ribenboim's range).

checked_by.who: R. G. E. Pinch (and P. Ribenboim for the 25 × 10^9 range)
checked_by.qualification: Number theorists who published pseudoprime tables in a refereed conference proceeding (Pinch) and a book (Ribenboim).
checked_by.what_they_did: Computed the pseudoprime tables; the primary texts were not read. Wikipedia reports the results.

events.directly_checkable: The pseudoprime tables can be re-derived by a computer search over base-2 Fermat pseudoprimes. Not re-run here.
events.doubts: A search snippet (not opened) says an OEIS comment records that one Pinch count, the Euler–Jacobi count at 10^13 (A055551), was wrong and later corrected. That concerns a different count and does not bear on the repeated-factor claim. It is noted only as a reason to read the primary tables before relying on them.
events.direction: Neutral on existence. It is a partial finite restriction on the non-squarefree candidates.

events.what_happened: V. Shevelev, G. García-Pulgarín, J. M. Velásquez-Soto and J. H. Castillo, 'Overpseudoprimes, and Mersenne and Fermat numbers as primover numbers', arXiv:1206.0606 (submitted 4 June 2012). The abstract states that squares of Wieferich primes are overpseudoprimes to base 2. 'Overpseudoprime' is a different and stronger class from the congruence asked here, and the paper does not address c² | 2^(c−1) − 1 for composite c.
events.revisions: Journal of Integer Sequences vol. 15 (2012) per the EMIS URL in a search result; the PDF was not opened.
events.delivers: Squares p² of Wieferich primes (1093² and 3511²) are overpseudoprimes to base 2. This is about the overpseudoprime class, not the congruence. It does not show that 1093² or 3511² satisfies c² | 2^(c−1) − 1, which would need 1093⁴ (resp. 3511⁴) to divide 2^(c−1) − 1.

checked_by.who: V. Shevelev, G. García-Pulgarín, J. M. Velásquez-Soto, J. H. Castillo (authors)
checked_by.qualification: Number theorists; the later journal version appeared in the Journal of Integer Sequences.
checked_by.what_they_did: Authored the result. Refereeing is implied by journal publication only; not read.

events.direction: Neutral for the question. The squares of Wieferich primes are the first candidates a naive search would test, and this result shows they are overpseudoprimes, not that they satisfy the congruence.

events.what_happened: N. A. Carella, 'Results for Wieferich Primes', arXiv:1712.08166 (submitted 21 Dec 2017). The abstract, which I opened, says that the search covers p < 10^15, finds two base-2 Wieferich primes, and gives a probabilistic prediction for a further base-2 Wieferich prime in [10^15, 10^40]. It concerns primes only.
events.delivers: Heuristic only: predicts another base-2 Wieferich prime in [10^15, 10^40]. Not a proof, and it does not address composite c.
events.direction: Neutral. If the prediction holds, it adds candidate prime factors; it does not bear on existence directly.

events.what_happened: OEIS A376473, submitted by Thomas Ordowski on 24 Sep 2024 (terms extended by Amiram Eldar the same day): numbers k with 2^(2^(k−1)−1) ≡ 1 (mod k²) but 2^(k−1) ≢ 1 (mod k). This is a different congruence, with the exponent 2^(k−1) − 1 rather than c − 1 or c. Its comments say every term has a Wieferich prime factor (example 951481 = 271 × 3511) and that 1093 cannot divide a term. 20 terms are listed, up to 2377714473001.
events.revisions: OEIS sequence page; the 'last modified' footer on the page is site-wide and not specific to this sequence.
events.delivers: A neighbouring congruence with 20 listed terms, each with a Wieferich prime factor. It does not touch 2^c − 1 ≡ 1 (mod c²) for any c.
events.directly_checkable: The listed terms can be checked directly against the stated congruence. Not re-run here.
events.direction: Neutral to the question. It states the same necessary condition (a Wieferich prime factor) for a different congruence.

events.what_happened: L. Jones, 'Wieferich Primes and Monogenic Trinomials', arXiv:2605.13460 (submitted 13 May 2026). The abstract, which I opened, states that x^(2p) + 2x^p + 2 is monogenic if and only if the prime p is not a Wieferich prime. It concerns polynomial rings and primes only.
events.delivers: A statement about monogenicity of one polynomial family indexed by primes p. It involves no composite c and no pseudoprime statement.

events.what_happened: R. Laniewski, 'Radical defects, Wieferich primes, and the abc conjecture', arXiv:2609.00039 (submitted 29 Aug 2026). The abstract, which I opened, defines a 'radical excess' for coprime triples a + b = c and studies the Mersenne family (1, 2^m − 1, 2^m). It states that transgression holds exactly when 2^m − 1 is not squarefree, on exponents of density 47/210. It also says that an abc counterexample along the Mersenne line 'would require infinitely many Wieferich primes', which is a conditional statement. It works with composite exponents, but not with the congruence asked.
events.delivers: Concerns squarefreeness of 2^m − 1 for exponents m and an abc-type excess. It does not address c² | 2^(c−1) − 1 or 2^c − 2 for composite c.
events.direction: Neutral to the question. It uses Wieferich primes conditionally, and only for the abc question.

summary: No event since January 2024 settles or moves this question. The searches (46 queries, listed verbatim below, with about 20 page reads) found the congruence stated only in OEIS A298944, whose comment reads 'Composites c where a(n) = 1 could be called Wieferich pseudoprimes. Do any such composites exist?' and gives no answer. The page I opened was current on 11 Oct 2026 but gives no later status. Reduction, which is my own reasoning and not sourced except where noted: the congruence is equivalent to 2^c ≡ 2 (mod c²); even c fail for c ≥ 4; for odd c it is 2^(c−1) ≡ 1 (mod c²). Any prime p dividing such a c must be a base-2 Wieferich prime, because the order of 2 modulo p² must divide c − 1, while p does not divide c − 1; OEIS A001220 states a related necessary condition. So existence of c is equivalent to the Ordowski conjecture in OEIS A001220 restricted to composites: that conjecture says no n > 1 with n² | 2^(n−1) − 1 is composite, and the page states it is equivalent to 'no Wieferich pseudoprimes (WPSPs) exist'. The known Wieferich primes are 1093 and 3511. The Dorais–Klyve search (2011) and PrimeGrid's reported completion to 2^64 (29 Dec 2022, restated in OEIS 24 Sep 2024) show no others below those bounds. So a composite solution below 2^64 would have to be 1093^a·3511^b. c = 1093·3511 fails by a 2-adic argument: 1093 ≡ 5 (mod 8), so 2 is a non-residue mod 1093, so 4 divides ord_1093(2), while c − 1 ≡ 2 (mod 4). The cases 1093², 3511² and higher powers need a finer fact, that 1093 and 3511 are not 'double Wieferich' (2^(p−1) ≡ 1 mod p³); I believe this holds but did not check it. Consequence for the judging pass: a composite solution, if one exists, needs either a Wieferich prime above 2^64, which none is known to exist, or a higher-power factor of 1093 or 3511. Both are open. The 2^64 bound is a volunteer computation whose reliability an OEIS editor questioned in 2015; I found no independent check. The computation I intended to run to test the congruence directly for composites up to 3 × 10^6, and the products 1093^a·3511^b, was not run: the shell command was not approved in this session. Every claim above that depends on computation is therefore unverified by machine. Close calls: (a) whether the 2^64 claim should count as a restriction (it counts only if the run is trusted); (b) whether the Pinch and Ribenboim repeated-factor checks count as covering the question (they cover only non-squarefree pseudoprimes below 10^12 or 25 × 10^9, not squarefree candidates). AI: no source I opened credits any AI system with this problem, and no AI-specific search (queries 7, 14, 27, 28, 33, 34, 42, 43) returned an AI result on this congruence. Two unresolved leads could still bear on it. (i) AlphaProof Nexus (arXiv:2605.22763, submitted 21 May 2026): the paper says 'We used Gemini to autoformalize 492 open questions from the OEIS' and reports 'found proofs for 44 conjectures that a manual review found to be correctly formalized and previously unproven'; Appendix A.1 names the prover as 'Gemini 3.1 Pro'. OEIS Open (arXiv:2608.11941, 12 Aug 2026) is a benchmark of the same 492 Lean-formalised OEIS open conjectures, where language-model agents settled 147 (30%). A298944 is an OEIS open conjecture of this kind and could be among the 492. I could not establish that it is: the OEIS Open results explorer rendered only its title, the formal-conjectures OEIS folder listing was truncated at 100 files, and formal-conjectures/…/OEIS/298944.lean returned 404 (weak evidence of absence). (ii) OpenAI's openai/math release (reported as 6 Oct 2026, 722 manuscripts in 372 families, 'an unreleased internal OpenAI model'; one secondary source says 719 manuscripts): I read only part of the number-theory catalogue, and no visible title concerns pseudoprimes or Wieferich primes. The 'none found' flags above are therefore for the events I recorded, not a verdict on the whole problem. Neighbouring events are recorded as discounted, with reasons: a different congruence (A376473, Guedes–Machado, Jones, Laniewski). Carella (2017) is a heuristic.
competing_reading: A reader could take the PrimeGrid 2^64 completion, plus the absence of any known example, as strong evidence that no composite solution exists, and treat the question as effectively settled 'no'. The sources do not support that: the question is an existence question over all composites, nothing bounds the size of a composite c, and the 2^64 completion is a bound on the prime factors, not on c. The opposite reading is that the question is restricted to one congruence and might be settled by a finer argument (for example, showing 1093 and 3511 are not double Wieferich, plus a proof that no further Wieferich prime exists). No such argument appears in the sources, and the OEIS comment says the conjecture behind it is 'probably extraordinarily difficult'.
what_would_settle_it: Either a composite c with c² dividing 2^(c−1) − 1 (a base-2 Wieferich pseudoprime, checkable by one modular exponentiation), or a proof that none exists, which would also settle the OEIS A001220 Ordowski conjecture. Intermediate evidence: an independent verification of the PrimeGrid run to 2^64, or the discovery of a third Wieferich prime, which would open candidates but not decide them. For the AI question: the OEIS Open or AlphaProof Nexus lists, checked by A-number for A298944 and for any Wieferich or pseudoprime conjecture, with the accepted Lean proof and its status.

events.credibility_reason: OEIS editor noted the PrimeGrid results were not double-checked and the search was suspended in 2017 for unreliable testing; no independent verification of the 2^64 completion found.

judgement.why: The statement is a single existence question over all composites. The Wieferich-prime searches (Dorais–Klyve, PrimeGrid) and the Pinch/Ribenboim pseudoprime tables are finite checks that only restrict where a composite solution could hide, so they are instances (F5); they also all predate the snapshot.
